draft.title: Other measures of wellbeing
card: the number of babies who die before their first birthday, for every 1000 born alive. A high rate points to weak health care, nutrition and living conditions.
the share of adults who can read and write. It shows how far people have had access to education.
the share of people with clean drinking water and safe toilets. Without them, disease spreads more easily.
the number of doctors for every 1000 or 10 000 people. A low number suggests people may find it hard to get medical care.
draft.remember: Each measure shows one side of wellbeing, so using several gives a fuller picture of how countries differ.

a.q: A country has a very high infant mortality rate. Which side of wellbeing does this measure mainly show?
opts: Health and living conditions for young children
How many adults can read and write
How evenly income is shared between people
How many people own a mobile phone
a.why: Infant mortality counts babies who die before their first birthday, so it reflects health care, nutrition and living conditions. Literacy is tempting but it measures reading and writing in adults, which is a different side of wellbeing.
a.clue: Think about what is being counted: babies who die.

b.q: Country A and Country B have the same adult literacy rate. In Country A, 95% of people have clean water and safe toilets. In Country B, only 50% do. What does this tell us?
opts: Education access is similar, but B has weaker water access
Country A has more doctors per 1000 people than Country B
Country B has a higher infant mortality rate than Country A
Both countries have the same level of wellbeing overall
b.why: The equal literacy rates suggest similar access to education, but the water and sanitation figures differ, so B is weaker on that side. The infant mortality option is tempting, but the data given does not measure it, so it cannot be concluded. Using one measure alone would have hidden the difference.
b.clue: Match each option to the measures the data actually gives.

a.best: Health and living conditions for young children

b.best: Education access is similar, but B has weaker water access
